strengths: FoNE is a simple, intuitive, and potentially useful representation: digit-aligned Fourier components encode numerical values compactly while avoiding multi-token fragmentation.

The synthetic arithmetic results are striking. FoNE reaches near-perfect or perfect exact-match accuracy across addition, subtraction, multiplication, classification, and modular-arithmetic experiments, often with substantially less data than the reported baselines.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this topic, including parameter/data scaling, efficiency measurements, alternative architectures, ablations, long-number addition, integration with Abacus, continual pretraining, and 10B-token language-model pretraining.
The one-token representation and parallel decoding provide meaningful computational advantages for number-heavy sequences, and the manuscript is generally clear and visually well organized.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the embedding contribution from the specialized output interface. FoNE predicts all digits in parallel using dedicated pairs of hidden coordinates and a fixed ten-class decoder, whereas digit-wise and subword baselines appear to generate multiple tokens autoregressively. This gives FoNE a much shorter sequence, direct per-position supervision, and an easier output problem. A crucial missing control is a one-token, parallel multi-head digit classifier with learned digit embeddings or other simple codes, using exactly the same input/output protocol.

The theoretical LayerNorm claim is not established for the implemented model. Lemma D.2 assumes zero mean, unit norms, orthogonality between FoNE and positional embeddings, and omits the added [NUM] embedding; none of these assumptions is shown to hold. Mean subtraction and additive embeddings can alter the angles used for recovery. Thus the statement that FoNE is unaffected by LayerNorm is substantially stronger than the proof supports.

Most headline evidence comes from IID synthetic arithmetic with fixed digit ranges. There is limited testing of extrapolation to unseen lengths, operand distributions, operations, or natural quantitative reasoning. The 60-digit experiment trains on length combinations up to the evaluated range, while the strongest length-generalization experiment switches to digit-wise FoNE plus Abacus rather than the proposed single-token system.

The claimed general-purpose numerical interface leaves important cases unresolved: negative numbers, signs, variable precision, leading zeros, scientific notation, identifiers, dates, units, and preservation of original surface forms. A parser that canonicalizes every detected number can erase semantically relevant formatting, and fixed maximum integer/fractional lengths constrain deployment.

The language-modeling evidence does not fully support the claim that semantic ability is preserved or improved. Ordinary token-level perplexity is not directly comparable across tokenizations, the text-only perplexity protocol is underspecified, and the full one-token FoNE method is not tested in the continual-pretraining experiment. MMLU alone, with essentially unchanged scores, is weak evidence for broad semantic preservation.

Reporting is insufficient for judging robustness and reproducibility: most headline curves lack error bars or multiple-seed summaries, the extensive method-specific hyperparameter searches are not documented, and optimizer, schedules, initialization, data-generation seeds, checkpoint selection, and executable code are not provided. Some appendix algorithms also contain ambiguous or shadowed indices.

Several claims are overstated. Exact mathematical invertibility under bounded precision does not imply that a transformer can robustly use the representation; the construction is redundant because the largest-period component is already injective over the bounded range; and the reported speed/data advantages conflate the encoding with hard-coded decimal structure and parallel decoding. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but fair matched-interface baselines and stronger out-of-distribution/general-language validation are needed for acceptance.

strengths: FoNE is a simple, intuitive structured representation: multi-scale sinusoidal features provide a compact, deterministic encoding of fixed-precision numbers, paired with a parallel digit-classification decoder. The synthetic arithmetic results are extensive and often strong, covering addition, subtraction, multiplication, modular arithmetic, data/model scaling, 60-digit addition, and combination with Abacus embeddings.

The paper considers efficiency as well as accuracy. Representing a number by one sequence token can materially shorten number-heavy contexts, and the reported training and inference savings are potentially useful.
The authors include several relevant ablations and make unusually substantial attempts to test language-model integration through 10B-token pretraining and 15B-token continual pretraining.
weaknesses: The principal arithmetic comparison is substantially confounded. FoNE receives a specialized fixed-width, parallel digit decoder, whereas digit-wise and subword baselines must autoregressively emit several tokens. This changes the output factorization and supplies digit-position structure in addition to changing the input embedding. Consequently, the results do not isolate the value of the proposed Fourier representation. Strong controls would include parallel digit heads using learned digit/positional features and other invertible structured encodings under exactly the same loss and decoder.

The language-modeling evidence is not valid as presented. Per-token perplexities are compared across tokenizations that produce different sequence lengths and output spaces, so the values in Figure 5 and Table 5 are not directly comparable. Byte-, character-, or document-normalized likelihood is needed. Moreover, the continual-pretraining experiment uses a simplified subword-level variant rather than the claimed single-token method, and MMLU alone does not establish preservation of semantic abilities.

The theoretical contribution is weak and partly unsound. Lemma 3.3 is the elementary invertibility of a point on a circle modulo its period, while the largest-period component alone already determines a bounded fixed-precision number in exact arithmetic. Lemma D.2 assumes zero mean, unit norms, and orthogonality between FoNE and positional encoding—conditions not shown to hold in the actual model. Standard LayerNorm subtracts a generally nonzero mean, so it is not merely uniform scaling and does not preserve the coordinate ratios invoked by the argument. Adding the learned [NUM] embedding further invalidates the claimed direct recoverability.

The method is much less general than the presentation suggests. It requires globally fixed integer and fractional widths and provides no clear treatment of signs, variable precision, leading zeros, scientific notation, NaN/Inf, ranges, dates, identifiers, or preservation of surface form. Canonical parsing can collapse semantically distinct strings, and the digit decoder lacks an explicit mechanism for predicting number length or formatting. Removing all numeric tokens from a BPE vocabulary is also not straightforward because many pieces are shared with nonnumeric strings.

The headline claims overstate scalability and generality. For long numbers, the representation is chunked and its dimensionality grows linearly with the maximum digit count, despite continuing to be called a single token. The main evaluations are IID synthetic arithmetic with fixed lengths and formats; there is little convincing evaluation on natural quantitative reasoning, tables, scientific data, or out-of-distribution values and precisions.

Experimental reporting is insufficient for the strength of the claims: most headline results lack multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and complete hyperparameter/search details; dataset disjointness is not established clearly; the numeric parser, mixed vocabulary/numeric loss, and perplexity computation are underspecified; and no code or artifacts are provided. Comparisons to fine-tuned Llama models are also difficult to interpret because objectives, decoding interfaces, training budgets, and degrees of task-specific structure differ.

Several results and explanations are internally questionable. For example, period 8 reaches 99.97% on base-5 inputs, weakening the asserted need to match the numeral base; bases 11 and 12 perform nearly perfectly on addition/subtraction, complicating the claimed base-10 sweet spot; and the claim that regression is incompatible with language modeling is contradicted by hybrid methods such as the included xVal baseline. Algorithm 3 also contains ambiguous digit indexing and overloaded variables.

Overall, the paper contains a promising engineering idea and notable preliminary results, but the unfairly coupled representation/decoder comparison, invalid cross-tokenization perplexity comparison, restrictive interface, and flawed normalization theorem leave the central claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier venue. These are major issues requiring redesigned experiments rather than minor revisions.

strengths: FoNE is a simple, novel, and potentially useful representation: digit-aligned Fourier features provide a deterministic single-position encoding, paired with an efficient parallel digit decoder.

The arithmetic experiments provide strong concrete evidence. FoNE substantially improves exact-match accuracy, data efficiency, parameter efficiency, and runtime over digit-wise tokenization, subword tokenization, XVAL, and NTL across addition, subtraction, and multiplication.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark and includes period and encoding ablations, a second transformer architecture, modular arithmetic, 60-digit addition, and integration with Abacus embeddings.

The 10B-token pretraining experiment and continual-pretraining study are valuable preliminary evidence that the approach can coexist with ordinary language modeling rather than serving only as an arithmetic-specific model.
weaknesses: Most decisive results use synthetic IID tasks with fixed digit ranges. Evaluation on length extrapolation, distribution shifts, negative numbers, varying precision, scientific notation, and realistic numerical-reasoning benchmarks is limited or absent; the 60-digit model is trained on operand lengths up to the evaluated range.

The specialized decoder assumes a predetermined number of digit positions and does not clearly handle signs, variable-length outputs, formatting, or uncertainty over numerical length. Calling the representation a single token also obscures that embedding and output dimensionality grow linearly with the maximum digit count.

Efficiency comparisons against autoregressive digit/subword baselines conflate representation with a materially different parallel output head. A baseline using ordinary digit features with the same parallel classification head would better isolate the value of the Fourier encoding.

Perplexities are compared across tokenizations without byte-, character-, or word-normalized likelihood. Moreover, training each method for 10B of its own tokens may expose models to different amounts of raw text, so this experiment does not by itself establish improved language modeling.

The theoretical support is weaker than presented. The invertibility lemma is elementary, while the LayerNorm lemma assumes zero mean, orthogonal unit-norm positional features, and uniform scaling; standard LayerNorm performs mean subtraction and learned coordinate-wise affine transformations, so the claimed invariance does not generally follow.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or generated datasets are provided, hyperparameter-search ranges are unspecified, and most headline experiments lack multi-seed uncertainty estimates. Some model descriptions and figure captions are also inconsistent about whether a 38M configuration or a 1B model is trained from scratch.
